analysis.title: Midterm update: Test of Democratic progressive movement's strength
key_insights: One week before the 3 November US midterm elections, Polymarket gives Democrats winning both chambers a 65.5% probability, the most likely outcome.

A contest between progressives and moderates inside the Democratic Party could affect fiscal policy under the next US government. Danske expects progressive candidates to be less inclined to push through policies that address persistently elevated budget deficits.

Strong results for progressive candidates could pose a marginal risk of further increases in public debt ratios compared with moderate candidates. Budget effects over the next two years would be limited.
If Democrats flip the House, as they are widely favoured to do, US fiscal policy is essentially locked in for 2027-28 regardless of the Senate result, because of presidential veto powers.

Strong progressive results could lead to a push for more influence and a progressive 2028 presidential candidate such as Ocasio-Cortez. Weak results would strengthen the case for a moderate such as Newsom or Ossoff.

In the Senate, progressive Democrats are favoured in Minnesota (Flanagan 86%), Michigan (El-Sayed 69%) and Maine (Jackson 61%). In Florida, progressive candidate Nixon has a 10% chance against incumbent Republican Senator Moody.

Per Kalshi, progressive Democrats are favoured to flip four of seven competitive House seats: California-22 (91%), Colorado-8 (84%), Pennsylvania-7 (87%) and Michigan-7 (73%). They are slight underdogs in Montana-1 (45%) and Maine-2 (45%), and have an 18% chance in Tennessee-9.

Texas is probably the most closely watched Senate race, with Democrat Talarico favoured to flip the seat at 66%. It would be the first Democratic statewide win in Texas since 1994. Polymarket puts the chance of a Democratic flip in Kansas at 38%.
